title: New psychology research sheds light on why certain pop song hooks stick in your head
excerpt:
Listeners judge musical hooks in unfamiliar pop songs as more attention-grabbing and memorable when they hear the songs multiple times, while an auditory verbal distraction makes those hooks feel less catchy, according to new research published in Psychology of Music . Across two laboratory experiments, chorus sections consistently stood out over other parts of a song even when listeners were distracted, suggesting that catchy pop phrases rely on both songwriting structure and human memory and attention.

In popular music, a hook is a distinct melodic, rhythmic, or lyrical phrase that grabs a listener’s attention and sticks easily in memory, such as the repeating nonsense syllables in Kylie Minogue’s “Can’t Get You Out of My Head.” Because modern pop recordings layer vocals, drums, bass, and harmonies all at once, the brain cannot process every detail equally and instead filters for standout moments. Researchers think these phrases lodge in verbal working memory, the short-term mental workspace often described as an “inner voice” that lets people silently rehearse words and melodies.
